standard.title: Language of evaluation and emotion
standard.description: understand how the language of evaluation and emotion, such as modal verbs, can be used to express and respond to opinions
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explore how language is used to appreciate texts and give reasons for preferences (AC9E2LA02). They have not yet examined the specific language resources — modal verbs, evaluative adverbs/nouns/verbs, and emotional language — that enable expressing degrees of certainty and responding to opinions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students understand how modal verbs, evaluative vocabulary and emotional language are used to express and respond to opinions.

nodes.label: Modal verbs and degrees of certainty
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify modal verbs and explain what degree of possibility, probability or necessity each expresses.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two modal verbs (e.g. 'must', 'might', 'could') and explain the different degree of certainty or possibility each signals.
nodes.typical_width: Explore how modal verbs indicate degrees of possibility, probability and necessity — distinguishing high modality ('must', 'will') from medium ('should', 'would') and low ('might', 'could') — and explain how the choice changes the strength of an opinion or claim.
wider: Compare how the same sentence changes meaning when different modal verbs are substituted, and discuss what this reveals about how writers signal confidence in their claims
Find examples of modal verbs in persuasive texts (e.g. advertisements, arguments) and analyse how modality is used to make claims seem stronger or more flexible

response_modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a repertoire of modal verbs across the certainty scale before they can use or analyse them flexibly. Building familiarity with examples from high to low modality is the prerequisite for understanding degree.

success_criteria: Student identifies a modal verb and names the degree of possibility/necessity it signals (high/medium/low)
Student explains how swapping one modal for another changes the strength of the statement

nodes.label: Evaluative and emotional vocabulary
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify evaluative and emotional vocabulary choices and explain how they express the speaker's or writer's feelings and opinions about characters, events or ideas.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify evaluative or emotional word choices in a text (adverbs, nouns or verbs) and explain what opinion or feeling each expresses.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise how adverb, noun and verb choices present different evaluations of characters and events; explore emotional language that demonstrates a range of emotions and positions; build vocabulary for expressing opinions and feelings.
wider: Compare how the same character is described with different evaluative vocabulary in two versions of the same story, and discuss what this reveals about point of view
Create a short text about the same event from two different emotional perspectives, choosing vocabulary deliberately to show the different positions

response_modes.reason: Students often see emotional vocabulary as simply positive or negative. Exploring different text types — narrative, persuasion, news — and different versions of the same story reveals that evaluative language constructs a specific perspective, not just a mood.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Evaluative vocabulary is a rich site at Y3: the connection between word choice and point of view is genuinely accessible and extends directly into both reading and writing. Exploring different versions of familiar stories (the wolf elaboration from LE01 is a natural link) makes this pedagogically engaging.
success_criteria: Student identifies evaluative or emotional vocabulary and names the opinion or feeling it expresses
Student explains how the word choice shows the speaker's/writer's position — not just that it describes the character or event
